speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: MOVEMENTS FROM THE WEST-STORAGE FOR NEXT SEASON
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask a question of the Minister of Agriculture concerning a matter of some urgency. What is being done to assist eastern farmers in obtaining from the west the necessary supplies of feed grains, of which there seems to be a scarcity?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture) :
subtopic: MOVEMENTS FROM THE WEST-STORAGE FOR NEXT SEASON
speechtext:
A number of inquiries have come in from eastern Canada having to do with the possibility of obtaining feed grains with which to finish live stock. There has been some difficulty getting feed grain moved from the west to the east. Those who make the inquiries would seem to have the opinion that there is a shortage somewhere. There is a vast quantity of feed grain in Canada that may be moved to the areas in which it is required. The difficulty is one of obtaining cars with which to move it. We have been accustomed to moving feed grain east, on the lakes, during the summer months, and having it stored in storage warehouses in Toronto and elsewhere for use in the winter months. That was not done to the same extent last year as in preceding years, possibly partly because the government pays the freight. The farmers are compelled to depend upon getting their feed in carload shipments from Fort William in the winter months. The hard winter with its heavy snow-falls created difficulties in moving the feed, but arrangements have been made with the railway companies to get as many cars as possible for that purpose.
There seems also to be the view that grain is being allowed to go to the United States, rather than to feeders in eastern Canada. That is scarcely true either. Feeders in the United States are having at least as much difficulty in having grain shipped into the United States as is being experienced by eastern Canadian farmers in having the grain shipped to eastern Canada. The reason is a shortage of cars on both sides of the boundary line.
An effort is being made at the present time to take care of the situation until such time as boats begin to move on the lakes. I should like to emphasize the importance of farmers and dealers, immediately that happens, making provision this summer for storing as much feed as they can during the summer months. There is a great supply of good feed grain available to be moved in the summer from the west, and if it is stored on farms or other storage warehouses throughout eastern Canada before close
[Mr Shaw.]
of navigation it will be helpful in producing results next year. Every possible effort, including a preference in movement east, is being made, and we are getting assistance from the United States to secure cars from that country to move grain south without interfering with the facilities necessary to move grain east.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I mentioned a day or two ago that it was hoped we might be able to begin the Easter recess on Friday of this week. I have been careful, on each occasion that I have referred to the Easter recess, to say that whether we would adjourn on Friday evening would depend upon the progress we might make between the time of the making of the statement and Friday evening. I must say it looks at present as though it were not going to be possible by that time to get before the deputy of his excellency for assent, the bills arising out of the resolutions on the budget. The government is most anxious, if at all possible, to have royal assent given to these measures before the Easter recess. If we are able to conclude the discussions in both houses on the resolutions, and have the bills ready for royal assent on either Friday or Saturday of this week, we may find it possible to adjourn for the Easter recess this week. If not, it will be necessary, I think, for us to continue on into next week-and as

Price Control
far into next week as may be necessary to make the progress we should like to have made.
The leader of the opposition has asked me what further legislation the government may have to bring down, notice of which has not already appeared on the order paper. The government will require a little time to give thought to some of the measures which may still have to be introduced before the close of the session. One purpose of having a recess of a fortnight, as I explained some time ago, is to afford the government that opportunity. In the circumstances it is intended, whenever adjournment comes, to hold to a recess of a fortnight. But whether that recess will begin on Friday night or some day next week will depend upon the progress we may make from now on. I am not in a position now, nor shall I be in a position until after the recess, to answer my hon. friend's question. However, after the Easter recess I shall seek to give the house such information as I may then be in a position to give with respect to the question the leader of the opposition has asked.

Mr. DOUGLAS G. ROSS (St. Paul's): On Monday, April 12, I asked a question in connection with the liability of automobile owners who were carrying members of the armed forces as passengers. My question was:
Has the Department of Justice given any opinion as to the liability of an automobile owner in case of an accident to a member of the armed forces while being driven as a passenger?
The answer of the Minister of National Defence was:
The answer is in the affirmative.
Will the minister have that opinion tabled?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. RALSTON (Minister of National Defence):
maintopic: LIABILITY OF AUTOMOBILE OWNER CARRYING MEMBERS OF ARMED FORCES AS PASSENGERS
speechtext: That whole matter is under consideration, along with the matter referred to yesterday by the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) regarding the action which is to be taken in view of the judgment of Mr. Justice Thorson respecting the non-liability of the crown for accidents due to the negligence of members of the forces while driving cars. I do not know that there is any particular objection to bringing down the opinion from the point of view of its contents. Sometimes opinions are brought down, and sometimes they are not brought down. I myself feel that it is a matter perhaps of concession to bring down opinions which are given by the law officers of the crown, and when I tell my hon. friend and the house that the very matter is being considered, along with the other question, perhaps that will be sufficient for him.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Munition? and Supply):
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when the committee rose last night I had discussed the steps which were being taken by the government to obtain immediate supplies of crude oil from Canadian sources, and I had also

Income War Tax
discussed the claims of discrimination against the so-called royalty companies. I should like to discuss the points that have been raised, which suggest discrimination against Turner valley producers in the matter of the price of crude oil in that area.
It has been suggested that subsidies have been paid on oil brought in from another country. The fact is that no subsidies have been paid by any agency on crudes imported into western Canada prior to April 1, 1943. The importations of crudes during the last several months have been in small quantity, and the refineries were able to absorb the extra cost. Now, however, when the quantity must be increased in order to satisfy our demands we are obliged to move farther afield than Montana, namely, to Wyoming and Kansas. The situation has changed-costs are greater and a subsidy must be paid. The primary duty of the office of oil control is that of supply, and this supply must be obtained from whatever source is available, regardless of increased costs.
Immediately prior to the war, the price of Turner valley crude oil was related competitively with the price of Cut Bank, Montana, crude oil, with the result that the laid down cost of Turner valley crude was approximately the same at Saskatchewan refineries as the laid down cost of Montana crude, adjusted for differences in quality. Since the outbreak of the war the oil controller has authorized two increases in the price of Turner valley crude oil, totalling 42 cents per barrel, of which 27 cents was authorized on July 16, 1941, and 15 cents on April 1,1943. 'The Cut Bank, Montana, crude price, on the other hand, has been increased by only 20 cents per barrel in United States funds, which compares with increases of 20 cents per barrel in United States gulf fields, and 15 cents in mid-continent and east Texas fields. Therefore the price increases permitted for Turner valley crude are greatly in excess of those enjoyed by any other producing field in the United States. There is no discrimination in this connection.
Cut Bank, Montana, crude now costs more at Regina refineries than Turner valley oil, notwithstanding the greater price increase permitted with respect to the latter. This may be attributed to war exchange tax, exchange on United States funds and slightly higher freight rates, all of which have occurred as the result of the war. When the western producer charges that there is a price discrimination because of the higher laid down cost of imported crudes, he is contending that the domestic price should include war exchange tax and foreign exchange. Obviously if the domestic price reflected these factors, the 72537-1374
consumer price would have to be increased accordingly, with the result that the prairie consumer would be paying an import tax and foreign exchange directly to the producer. Obviously also this would not be fair to the consumer, and if permitted the consumer could very well charge discrimination.
As to discrimination because of the payment of subsidies, it is obvious that someone must pay for the more costly oil which Turner valley is unable to produce. These expenses must be paid for by the consumer, the refiner, the domestic producer, or the government by way of subsidies. There is no intention of recommending that the consumer price ceilings be punctured. If refineries were asked to absorb the increasing financial burden of this outside supply, it would prevent them from paying the higher price for Turney valley crude. It was therefore decided to subsidize the additional cost of the imported crude which had to be obtained to meet our requirements and ask the refineries to pay the highest price possible for domestic production, within consumer price ceilings. The payment, therefore, of subsidies on imports is not discriminating against the Turner valley producer; on the contrary, the payment of subsidies made possible a substantial increase in production revenue.
The whole question of price discrimination may be summed up in the proposition whether or not the prairie farmer, who is also a producer, should pay the Turney valley producer war exchange tax and foreign exchange on his production. There should be no difficulty in anticipating the consumer's answer to this proposition.
At the last sitting of the committee I promised to make a statement on the obtaining of oil from the tar sands of northern Alberta. I will do so at this time.
There seems to be an erroneous idea in the minds of many regarding these tar sands. Whether these ideas are due to propaganda, supported by wishful thinking, I do not know. Judging by what one hears at times, one would think that oil is running out of these sands, and that all that has to be done is to tap or pipe the oil, and this country would overcome its serious oil shortage. The facts do not bear out any such idea.
While I make this statement, I do not wish to suggest that these tar sands have not possibilities. They may have, but many problems must be solved before anything can be produced which will have real beneficial value.
I know of no more aggressive body of men in industry than those directing the large oil companies. They have explored all likely
Income War Tax

areas in the world to obtain supplies of this precious product, oil, and it is significant to know that they have turned away from these sands rather than undertake the solution of the many problems incident to their development, and the production of products equal in quality and which can be sold at competitive prices with the same products procured elsewhere.
For thirty years the tar sands of Alberta at and around McMurray, have been under investigation. by engineers of the Department of Mines and Resources.
While it was known that there are large deposits of these sands, there were, and still are, many problems to be solved before they can be commercialized and/or can be used to produce marketable products such as gasoline, diesel oil, fuel oil, et cetera.
The following problems had to be solved:
(1)	Economic methods of mining the sands.
(2)	Separation of bitumen from the sands.
(3)	Treatment of the bitumen after it is separated to produce marketable products.
(4)	Removal, or at least substantial reduction of the high sulphur content of the crude products obtainable from the extracted bitumen. With the high sulphur content of the bitumen, there is consequently high sulphur in the lighter fractions, i.e. gasoline, diesel oil, et cetera. This sulphur must be removed to obtain marketable products.
(5)	A thick uniform rich deposit of sands with a light overburden had to be located.
(6)	A solution had to be found for the disposal of the overburden and waste so as not to pollute any navigable stream or body of water. When it requires a ton of sand to produce a little less than a barrel of bitumen, in a deposit of the type on Horse river, the magnitude of the tonnage of tailings to be disposed of can be understood more readily.
(7)	Transportation had to be found for the movement of the. products to the market at reasonable cost.
Since 1913 field and laboratory investigations have been carried on by the federal Department of Mines and Resources. These included laboratory studies of methods for separating the bitumen from the sand and refining of the bitumen by cracking and hydrogenation for the production of sulphur-free commercial products.
In 1926 four reservations, aggregating 2,068 acres, were made by the parks branch of the dominion government in order to ensure an adequate supply of road surface material for national parks.

In 1930 the national resources, including these tar sands, were transferred by the dominion to the province of Alberta, reserving, however, for the parks branch, the 2,06S acres before mentioned.
In the year 1930, Max W. Ball of Denver, Colorado, entered into an agreement with His Majesty King George V, represented by the minister of the Department of the Interior, which department has since been amalgamated with the Department of Mines and Resources, to mine bituminous sands on the Horse river block and to extract therefrom the bitumen and other hydrocarbons contained therein, on a basis whereby a share of the resulting products would belong to His Majesty for the benefit of national parks. This original agreement was superseded by an agreement entered into on February 18, 1935. This agreement was later assigned to the Canadian Northern Oil Sand Products Limited. This company changed its name by supplementary letters patent under date of April 25, 1935, the name of the new company being Abasand Oils Limited. The present agreement was entered into on February 18, 1942.
In 1935, preparations were made by Abasand Oils Limited for the construction of a 250 tons per day separation plant on Horse river. This plant was completed in September, 1936; it operated a short time, sufficient only to indicate that certain modifications were necessary. A road was also constructed by this company from the plant to Waterways.
In 1937, an enlargement of the plant to 400 tons per day capacity, together with a refinery, was commenced on the same site. Due to difficulties in mining the sand, construction was discontinued temporarily and resumed in 1939. This plant was finally completed in 1940. Subsequently, a small pipeline was built to Waterways, which is the terminal of the railroad from Edmonton, and the shipping point for northern areas.
Production began again in May, 1941, but again mining difficulties were encountered and production fell. Further, there were only intermittent operations.
In November, 1941, the separation plant and power house was destroyed by fire and all production ceased. In 1942, the plant was rebuilt.
By agreement of February 18, 1942, Abasand Oils Limited was granted the exclusive right to a tract consisting of 100 acres, being part of the 581 acres on Horse river, and retained by the federal government for parks purposes; further, to have the right to mine and process bituminous sands therefrom, to sell and transport products made from these sands and erect such buildings and install such equipment as

Income War Tax
necessary. The operator undertook: (a) to erect on the tract a plant capable of extracting the bitumen from 250 tons of sand per day; (b) to erect and equip a refinery in the province of Alberta to manufacture gasoline, asphalt and other products, to the satisfaction of the Minister of Mines and Resources; (c) to mine and treat 25,000 tons of sand in the year 1942, subject to certain terms and conditions set forth in detail in the agreement itself.
The oil controller was appointed in June, 1940. and in July of the same year had his first meeting with offiicals of Abasand Oils Limited. At that date the Abasand officials were satisfied that they had developed the McClave process for the separation of the bitumen from the sands to a point where they could proceed with the solution of the other problems involved. At that time the problem of mining the sands was giving them serious concern. They were developing a shale planer. Within a few months, however, this method proved a failure and was abandoned. Shortly after, operations ceased for that year.
Again, in the spring of 1941, Abasand Oils Limited renewed activities -towards a solution of their many -problems; mechanical difficulties were constantly encountered. As a result, a continuous run of the plant was impossible, and it was out of the question to procure a sample of the bitumen required for research purposes. In the- fall, as hereinbefore stated, this plant was burned down and, naturally, all operations had to be suspended.
Owing to the urgency of -the situation and in the hope of speeding up the solution of the many problems ye-t to be, dealt with, the government entered' into an agreement with the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company-the cooperation of Abasand Oils Limited was secured-and an appropriation of $75,000 was made to carry out the work. This appropriation was later increased to $200,000. Consolidated Mining and Smelting company undertook the work without profit, but on the assurance that they would1 suffer no loss. We were assured by Abasand Oils Limited that their plant would be reconstructed early in the summer and that they would be in a position to carry on a continuous operation, from which we could make studies of the success of the McClave process, et cetera, and procure samples to determine what products -could be produced from the bitumen, and estimate costs of the operation. To this end) negotiations were -carried on by the oil controller with the office of the petroleum administrator for war in Washington, with a view to having organizations in the United
States make thermal and catalytic cracking, and hydrogenation tests of the samples, particularly in respect to the possibility of obtaining aviation gasoline, motor gasoline, diesel oil and fuel oil. As a result, arrangements were made for laboratory tests by Universal Oil Products of Chicago on thermal and catalytic cracking, and by Standard Oil Development Company of Baton Rouge on hydrogenation. Inasmuch as hydrogenation on a large scale would require an expenditure of possibly $12,000,000 or more, the research by Universal Oil Products on thermal and catalytic cracking was considered advisable, since, if it were successful, the cost-although substantial-would be less. The great advances made in all refining operations, particularly since the war, unquestionably should-help in the solution of the refining an-d sulphur reduction problems. *
Unfortunately the plant of Abasand Oils Limited, as reconstructed after the fire, could only operate intermittently, and the information we hoped to get from this plant was not obtainable.
Further, owing to bottlenecks in the plant, we were unable to procure samples of the bitumen of the type required for research investigation to give the quickest results, and we were unable to procure the quantity of bitumen necessary for the plant test at Baton Rouge.
Details of the highlights of the agreement with Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company Limited were the following:
Under this agreement the company undertook :
(a)	Test drilling of the bituminous sand areas in the vicinity of Fort McMurray, Alberta, to provide reliable information as to the location of areas which might support large-scale developments for production of oil on the scale of 10,000 to 20,000 barrels per day;
(b)	Study of the plant of Abasand Oils Limited with regard to costs, efficiency, et cetera;
(c)	Research to discover the kinds and qualities of products that could be produced from the bitumen.
The report of Consolidated reads in part as follows:
Deposit. There are tremendous deposits of oil sands in the McMurray area, but much of this area is overlain by heavy overburden and lean oil sands. The exploration problem was to find an area with a large tonnage of high grade sand under light overburden with necessary natural advantages for a plant.
Two areas judged from previous work to be most promising were selected for drilling. The drilling done shows clearly that the deposits
Income War Tax

are generally interlayered with clay and lean sand and vary widely within short distances, both horizontally and vertically to a greater degree than had been expected.
We are of the opinion from the results to date, that large tonnages of high grade sand 

about 16 per cent bitumen and 5 per cent minus 200 mesh-similar to that now being treated by Abasand will not be readily found. Large tonnages of sand containing about 12 per cent bitumen and high in minus 200 mesh material-25 per cent-could probably be readily blocked out. Until complete data on capital cost, operating costs and details of products which can be produced are available, it is impossible to determine the minimum grade of sand that will make an operation a practical proposition. In any case from the operating costs quoted later it will be seen that a thorough search for a high grade deposit is very desirable.
Then come the reports on two areas, the Wheeler Island and the Steepbank river areas.
From whose report has the minister quoted?
Has it been taken over under -the arrangement the minister mentioned last night, that it will be handed back to the company?

Yes, we are simply taking it over to conduct certain experiments. We hope to recover from paving material produced for the Alaska highway the costs we expend, and the property will not be returned until the money is recovered.
But after the process has been developed the plant will be handed back to the company?
At that time we can either buy it or hand it back.

We take
the risk and the company subsequently takes [DOT]the profit?

Income War Tax

Well, there is no certainty of profit. What we are trying to do is to find a process for developing the sands. After the process is found we shall know whether it is more suitable for government or for private developme'nt. Perhaps that will be a matter for another minister to decide, at the rate this is going. In any event, we are taking any steps we believe will hasten the conclusion of the investigation. I sincerely hope we shall be able to find the solution of many problems by the autumn of this year. One difficulty is that the plant has never operated in the winter months; it has always been a summer operation. If no way can be found of making it a twelve months in the year operation, that will be a serious handicap. Efforts are being made to overcome the obstacles to winter operation. All "these things are being driven forward as rapidly as possible. We hope to have a small commercial operation, as a by-product of the research this summer, producing bituminous material for the Alaska highway, so that there will be some revenue to offset the expenditure. But one would have to be very optimistic to believe that we shall be able to start any large-scale construction before the spring of
1944.

Has any report been submitted to the minister by the national research council? I understand that a number of years ago a chemical engineer named Gower made some submission of formulae which he had worked out for extracting gasoline and oil from the tar. Has the minister any information on that?

The Department of Mines and Resources is working with us on this problem. Two or three experts of that department were on the ground the greater part of last summer; they were checking the operating results and advising on the location of test drilling. Another representative of the department is following the experimental work in laboratories in the United States. Everything that has been submitted to the Department of Mines and Resources, the vast amount of data they have accumulated over the years, is being checked. I would remind my hon. friend that for some thirty years the Department of Mines and Resources has been actively studying this situation. Every known process has been tried, and to-day I think the fact is that no satisfactory process either for mining the tar sands or for extracting the oil in an economical way has been wholly perfected.
Mr. MaeNICOL: Yesterday we listened to what I thought were two excellent speeches from the hon. member for Calgary East and the hon. member for Calgary West respectively. I was impressed by both. I gathered
from them that the independent companies in the Turner Valley were not being supported as they should be. If those statements are correct, as I have no doubt they are, since those two gentlemen come from the locality and must know the situation there, their statements were indeed alarming to me. After listening to the minister I am again much alarmed. I want to see oil produced in this country. If we have the resources, why do we import up to $100,000,000 worth of oil and its products yearly?
The minister read a report presented by the Consolidated Mining and Smelting company I have nothing but the highest respect for that company, but it is a gold mining company. I do not know what its experience has been with oil, or whether the engineers who deal with gold production are also qualified to produce oil. But when the government determined to make an investigation into the oil sands, why did they not send engineers from the Department of Mines and Resources to make the investigation? If the statement just made by the minister is correct then I cannot understand the statements that have been issued during the years by the Department of Mines and Resources.
Last summer I paid my second visit to Fort McMurray and spent several days at the little plant the minister has been reading about. While I was there I met one of the greatest oil geologists in the world, who is close to the chief of the department in Washington. He was strong in his praise of the possibilities of the oil sands on the Horse river and Athabaska river and that whole area. Other great engineers have been there, and they have all, so far as I know, stated that there is a vast volume of oil in that locality. Had Doctor Camsell, head of the Department of Mines and Resources, been sent up there or had he been requested to send his engineers to make an investigation, without passing any comment upon the report which has been made, I would have felt much better, because of the fact that the engineers of the Department of Mines and Resources have been off and on that job for many years. One of them, Doctor S. C. Ells-* the minister knows him very well-all down through the years since 1911 has stated, and backed up his statement with facts and figures, that there is a very large volume of oil there. I have the statement by Doctor Ells under my hand; it was to the effect that there are at least a hundred billion barrels of oil in that area. Of course he is careful to say that approximately a billion barrels are readily accessible. The hundred billion barrels, as the
Income War Tax

minister has said, are in sands about which, over which and under which are other kinds of sand or dirt.
I like to see things for myself, and I went over that area fairly comprehensively. 1 saw a great deal of oil sand, and in my hand at the moment I have a chunk of oil sand. While the report read by the minister would lead one to believe that there are very few areas with any large quantities of oil sand, my own observation is that on the Athabaska river there are many areas with large quantities of this sand. For the life of me I cannot understand what is blocking the production of oil in Canada in a large way, if I may use that expression to give my own opinion. Is some sinister influence at work? I do not know;
I do not say there is, but who is blocking the production of oil in a large way in Canada? Great English oil geologists have been up there and have stated in very strong. language that there is a very large volume of oil to be obtained in that locality. I believe Mr. Bosworth, of London, England, representing the Royal Geological Society, visited the Athabaska district and on his return to London made a somewhat startling statement at a meeting of that society. His statement was:
. . . should there never be a drop of oil found in a well in western Canada, there was enough oil in sight in the sands of the Athabaska river to supply the British empire for a thousand years.
I may add that I quoted what Mr. Bosworth said from a very old book pertaining to oil sands, entitled, "Particulars of Tar Sand Lease No. 15, known as the Murphy Claim," published in 1915, which also quotes statements made by Doctor Ells. Last June, however, Doctor Ells wrote another article in the Canadian Geographic Journal, in which he said:
Certain factors are definitely favourable to the production of crude oil from Alberta bituminous sands by methods now proposed, and, to a large extent, already demonstrated. Production of 30,000 barrels per day could be maintained over a period of not less than fifty years.
That is not a large production; it is nothing like the doctor's previous statement in regard to a hundred billion barrels, but even 30,000 barrels a day is worth while. I believe we are producing at Turner valley about 26,000 barrels per day.	[DOT]
The report read by the minister said something about sulphur. I heard about this some time ago; in fact I was told about it last summer or last fall by an engineer at Fort McMurray, not the engineer to whom I referred a few moments ago who came from

Washington, but another engineer. Since that time I have been making an investigation, as extensive as I can make it, into the r moval of sulphur from oil, and as to how much sulphur there is in oil produced from other sources. I find that the 'crude oil being refined here in Canada contains anything from -1 per cent up to 2-15 per cent of sulphur. In the reports of the sands on the Athabaska I find that the sulphur content varies, apparently depending on where the sample is taken. In one sample the sulphur content was 4-6 per cent; in another it was 1-5 per cent; in another it was as low as -3 per cent and in still another it was 3-0 per cent. The minister said something about Germany having the hydrogenation process for the removal of sulphur. I would not care what process was used, but if Canada is going into the oil business to produce oil in a large way, ini an endeavour to wholly eliminate the importation of $100,000,000 worth of oil a year, if $30,000,000 is the cost of a large plant using the German process, in my judgment that is not too much to spend for this purpose. Everyone knows that to-day Germany is producing its gasoline from lignite coal or from a brown grade of bituminous coal. Everyone knows that these coals contain sulphur to a large extent, at least to the extent of the oil sands of Alberta; yet Germany produces the highest grade of gasoline in this way. Further, we all know that benzol and benzine and naphtha, which are used to pep up German gasoline and give it -high performance-I presume these things are used here also-are also taken from the coal. So I am not a bit worried about having to remove sulphur from these oil sands. If we have the determination to take it out, we can take it out.
In regard to the mining end of it, as far as I could see last year they had pretty well overcome their mining troubles. They did have trouble when I was there two years ago, when, as the minister said, they were using scrapers. The difficulty was not that they could not scrape off the sand, but they could not produce enough scrapers to do it. When I was in business we used to sandblast iron, and I know the effect of sand on iron, so that after a few days their scrapers were finished. Last summer they were blasting it out, as they would blast in any other mine, and as far as I could see they were having great success. I believe they had about six rows of holes in depth and perhaps twenty-five or thirty in length along the face of the pit. They would blow them all off at one time, and it seemed to me to break up the sand into very small pieces. That had been

Income War Tax
their big trouble previously. As to the plant itself, I cannot say whether or not they were having satisfactory results, but I do know that engineers both at Yellowknife and at the Box mine on Athabaska lake told me that the diesel oil produced by Abasand was first class. Everyone knows that if there is much sulphur in diesel oil it will pit the valves of the diesel engines, and surely these engineers would not make the statement that the diesel oil was good if it was not good.
I am not blaming the minister for what has happened. I will say a word for him in a' moment, for I think he is trying to find out whatever he can. I should like to know, however, if there is any sinister influence blocking the production of oil in a big way in this country. At Abasand they take it out by a hot water process. I dio not know that that is a first class method, but the fact remains that they do seem to get the oil out of the sand. Some engineers say, however, that it is not as good as it should be. The hydrogenation process is better.
Someone mentioned Charles Gower of Regina. Last summer when I was in Regina I went to see a plant which had been operated by Charles Gower. I found him to be a bright young engineer. As a matter of fact he was at Abasand two years ago when I was there. He used a solvent method. Has that method been tried? I dlo not know. Is it being tried on the job? I do not know. I say the minister should make every effort in every possible way to produce oil. We have an oil controller who is doing good work, a man for whom I have the highest praise. But what we want is an oil producer. Why cannot the government nominate an oil producer, giving him power to produce oil? If oil is up there the minister should instruct a vigorous oil producer, with plenty of backing, to produce oil, just as it is now controlled. I am looking not only to the duration of the war but to the time after the war.
With our great oil resources goodness knows we must get out of the class of an oil importer. Our importations have been at the rate of about 8100,000,000 a year. If we have an oil producing plan, then we have the resources here from which to produce, and we might better use our own people to produce it.
Where are we to get the oil if we do not produce it? We produce only about 12,000,000 barrels a year in Canada. In fact we are one of the smallest oil producers in the world. Egypt is last with about 6,000,000 barrels, Bahrein about 7,000,000 and Burma about 6,000,000. Yet Canada, a country covering
half a continent, is one of the smallest producers. We heard last night about our oil resources, stretching right from the international boundary up into northern Alberta. It is about time we began to produce oil in this country in a large way.
There are three methods used. One is the hot water method, another is the Gower solvent method and the third is the situ method, where they drill a hole down through the sands and apply some kind of heating apparatus which melts the oil. They get it out in that way, although I do not think it is a good system. Then the last method is by hydrogenation.
The minister has full control of the situation. He is a vigorous minister, and does not allow anything to block him. If he is going to try to do something, he tries to do it. If he had to put in a hydrogenation process, even at a cost of some millions of dollars-[DOT] that is what they paid in the United States- I should not think it would be an insurmountable obstacle, if we were then able to produce oil in a big way. That is the whole object I have in mind, namely the production of oil in a big way.
I said a moment ago I would say a word for the minister. Last year I discussed this matter on June 29, and at that time he was very kind. After the house rose he did engage Consolidated Smelters to send engineers into that area. At the time I was there there were said to be thirty-two engineers on hand, and all of them were splendid men. I had met some of them before, and had the highest regard for them. The minister did that however, and also had something to do with trying to produce oil at Commotion creek in northern British Columbia. About $600,000 or $700,000 was spent there, and after drilling a well 6,000 or 7,000 feet oil was not found. Then, in the Pouce Coupe area of Alberta a large amount of money was spent, although I am not sure that it was spent by the .government. I have never heard what the results were. I talked to one of the engineers, who did not seem to be very optimistic. What the results were I cannot say.
Lately I have been speaking to the minister about trying to produce oil near Peace River, Alberta. I went down the Peace river quite a few miles, I have forgotten just how far. to see five wells. I have pictures here of those wells, and I also have pictures of Abasand. I might add that I take my own pictures. Those five wells were shooting oil, water and gas into the air about fifty feet. They were burning gas, just as we see it in

the Turner valley. To see that gas blazing away, twenty-four hours of the day since about 1912, strikes one as a shocking waste. On the Peace river the wells were drilled to around a thousand feet or more.
If I have any influence with the minister I suggest that he send someone to drill in Peace River area. Any operations carried on there could not be less successful than the drilling at Commotion creek. All I can say is that there are evidences of oil along the Peace river. The mere fact that five wells were drilled many years ago is evidence of that. I saw quite a lot of oil. There may be a lot of sulphur in oil lying on the top of the ground. It would seem, if we may judge from newspaper articles, that an oil shortage is anticipated in the United States. They have been producing about 1,350,000,000 barrels a year, or over half the total amount produced in the world. Whether they are trying to frighten us or not, I cannot say. However the newspapers recently carried the suggestion of an approaching oil shortage.
In the Montreal Daily Star under date of April 12 appears a short article entitled "Oil Shortage Ahead in the United States '. This article refers to a meeting then taking place in Detroit of the American Chemical Society, in which a speech was delivered by Doctor Benjamin T. Brooks, consulting chemist of New York city. Doctor Brooks went on to say that owing to dwindling resources of petroleum the United States will have to abandon the heating of residences by oil. That will be a serious problem over there, and also serious here. In the United States there are about 1,500,000 oil burners used in the heating of domestic buildings. I believe we have about 75,000 buildings in Canada in which oil-burning equipment is used. If we have to remove those oil burners, a cost of about $25,000,000 or $50,000,000 would be involved. I should think it would be more advisable to spend the same amount in the building of a hydrogenation plant to produce oil such as we find in the United States and in Germany.
Let us take note of what Germany has done in the matter of hydrogenation. They do not have gasoline supplies such as we have. They have not oil wells of much capacity and for that reason they process coal. I believe they were producing about 15,000,000 tons of oil per year from coal. They used the hydrogenation

process to obtain the gas. Their capacity would not give them more than about 80,000,000 barrels of gasoline, but it is possible that they have greatly increased their plant

I believe the minister is in earnest, and that he wishes to do the best he can. But I was alarmed when I heard the observations of hon. members from Calgary and, as I said at the beginning of my observations, I was alarmed when I heard the minister. I hope my cause for alarm is unfounded.
May I close with these remarks: Let nothing stop the minister from producing oil. He has been doing a fine job. If he has to do it, let him name an oil producer. He already has an oil controller to take care of that end of the matter. Clothe the oil producer with all the necessary power and tell him to go out and get the oil wherever he can and produce it in large volume. I am sure the mines and resources branch, Doctor Camsell and his engineers, will do the best they can to assist. If Canada has these resources, all that is needed is to put the country in a position to produce all the oil and gasoline we require and perhaps to export some of it.
Mr. COLDWELL; Some little time ago, having heard a statement made by a man in New York of international reputation regarding the tar sands in Alberta, I put on the record a portion of one of a series of lectures to which he referred me. I should like to refer to that this afternoon.
I listened with a great deal of interest to the statement made by the minister. It might be interesting to see just who Wallace E. Pratt is. After all, what a man is and what he does gives some clue as to how his opinion should be weighed. A few minutes ago I sent out and got a copy of

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: May I suggest to the hon. member that in a period of extremely high taxes, excess profit taxes such as we must have to-day, the development he speaks of is a natural one and does not reflect at all on the willingness of private enterprise to take risks under normal conditions. A system of taxation which takes most of the profits away, if there are profits, but would leave the company to take the losses, if there are losses, naturally has a dampening effect upon the desire of a company to take risks.

Of course the minister's viewpoint is governed by this fact, that he looks forward after the war to a diminution in demand for all kinds of consumer goods. Therefore the private company cannot be expected to take a risk which must carry over into the post-war period. That is' quite an understandable point of view.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not necessarily do that. There may be a change in demand that would have the same effect with many companies as a diminution of demand. All it means is that in a highly abnormal war period if taxation of the type of the excess profits tax is very high, as it has to be and as I believe it ought to be, you cannot reasonably expect private enterprise to take the risks which they otherwise would take, because if there are profits they cannot benefit from them.

I agree with what the minister has just said, but I am pointing out that so far as we are concerned we do not. believe that this is the proper way of doing public business. We believe that at the present time, under the pressure of war and the argument that the corporations are taking risks, we are handing over some of the most valuable concessions we have. There is not only this oil concession. There are the huge power resources, such as those at Shipshaw which are being taken out of the public domain and placed in perpetuity into the hands of private corporations, like the Aluminum company, which are tremendously strong and a tremendous menace to the people of this country. There is no more disreputable story of brigandage and of what is sometimes called in the United States robber barons than you will find in the history of the oil industry.
We are on resolution 16. Let us get back to the resolution.

I think my hon. friend misunderstands the situation. The proven area in Turner valley is comparatively limited in extent. It is definitely limited in the north and south ends and at the margins. There are, however, a limited number of sites in the proven area which have not been drilled. Provincial law defines the size of an area which warrants a well, and the sites I am speaking of are one-well sites. What we are trying to do is to drill out Turner valley to its full activity this year. There is immediate need of more production from that area. Imperial Oil agreed at once to drill out the remainder of the sites which they own, at their own expense. Other large companies did likewise. But there are certain areas there which are owned by companies which are simply owners of the lease. These are the so-called small men whom we are trying to help. We could not call on the owner to do the development because he is not in that type of business. That is the kind of site we intend to drill out.

I have no desire to get into a controversy this afternoon with the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar on questions of private enterprise when, by keeping silent, I can help the minister get his resolution through.
That would be a change.

The hon. member can sneer if he likes; but I venture to suggest, and I put myself on the judgment of the members of this house, whether I have not made more constructive suggestions in the three sessions which have passed than all the members of his group put together.
That is egotistical, if you like.
I put myself in the judgment of the house if I have not given more cooperation to the government than the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar and his whole group.
That is a matter of opinion.

I merely rise to emphasize what the minister has said, that in these days of extreme taxation, of 100 per cent excess profits, no private individual or private company can undertake the expansion of the natural resources of this country and shoulder all the losses and then give back to the government all the increase above a certain small minimum. It is not in the ordinary course of free enterprise that a man should go on under those circumstances; and as long as that position obtains-and it obtains because the nation is at war-private enterprise is throttled;. Neither the government nor anyone else can demand of such a one, "Yes, you can go on and make this investigation and incur this expenditure and achieve a success, but we will step in and take all the fruits of your labour. At the same time, and in the interests of the province from which I come, I would ask the minister to make a brief statement, either now or at a later stage, with respect to the Albert county oil shales. There is a good . deal of disappointment in New Brunswick because, in our search for oil, nothing has been done there. I know something about the situation. That may be justified.
I do not know. I do not press the minister to speak on the matter to-day if he has not the information here, but I ask him to make a statement at some time so that it will be put on the record.

May I take a few minutes of the time of the committee? I hesitate a great deal in doing so, because we are all anxious to proceed with this legislation a little more quickly than we have done so far. I have not hitherto occupied any time, either in committee or in the house; but as the tar sands to which references have been made are in the constituency which I have the honour to represent, I may be able to tel1

the hon. member for Davenport something not only about what has happened in the past two years in which he has taken an interest in this development, but about what has been done by the people of Edmonton and district and others, including myself, in the last thirty years for the development of these resources. If he wants to know something as to the paternity of this development process, I might remind him that it was a government of the political colour to which he belongs that in 1916 cancelled all our leases and made us lose every dollar we had invested in the McMurray Oil company and the Fort McKay Asphalt and Oil company. It was local capital, contributed by the people of Edmonton and district, which was invested in order to develop these great natural resources, but the last war had not gone on very long when, because of the statutes and regulations then put in force, we were unable to proceed any further. We pointed out then the very difficulties which have arisen lately, namely lack of men and of material, but our representations were made to no purpose. In contrast with the care and attention paid to the development of these resources and to the interests of local people, as exhibited by the present government and the present minister, the government of that day cancelled our leases and we lost all the money we invested. The effect was to retard development for many years. People with money were unwilling to take the risk of investing it in the development of the resources of the province of Alberta.
Just to put the record right, I have to disagree with the hon. member for Davenport, and to point out that it was in February of the last session that I brought up this matter by placing a resolution on the order paper asking the government to look into the development of the oil sand resources.
I cannot agree with the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation in his criticism of the present arrangement. Although I am inclined to believe that the government is proceeding a little too carefully, from the studies I have been able to make, and records I have from engineers as celebrated as those referred to by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, I am convinced that the possibility of the mining and the extraction of oil from those sands has been proved. I know also that lately an authority, whom I believe the minister mentioned in his statement, has declared to a shareholder of the Abasand Oil company, whose letter I have here, that the separation of the sulphur creates no great impediment, and that as a matter of fact in many fields in the United States,

though we have few in Canada, where the same condition exists, separation of the sulphur has been done at very little cost and has not prevented these fields from competing with others.
The paving qualities of the material were proved long ago. Hon. members who have travelled in Alberta may remember that for many years a part of what was formerly known as the Fort Saskatchewan trail out of Edmonton has been paved with the tar sands of the McMurray district.
It was built in 1911.

This pavement is still good and in constant use. Part of the main road leading to the parliament buildings in Edmonton is also paved with this material, which has proved just as good as any which was imported from Trinidad and other parts of the world.
I am disposed to agree with the hon. member for Davenport that we would be justified in going a little faster. The immensity of the field is proved. The location mentioned in the report is only one small percentage of the great field available. These tar sands extend all the way down the river to Fort McKay. I saw them years ago, long before the hon. member for Davenport knew there were tar sands in that region, long before the railway came. And these tar sands extend a considerable distance up the Clearwater river which falls into the Athabaska at Fort McMurray. I suggest to the minister that it would be a golden opportunity to use these tar sands for paving the Alaska highway. I know we are spending a large amount of money, but I appeal to hon. members who saw the picture this morning of the great battle in Egypt and Libya and from it got a conception of the tremendous organization entailed by this war, the immense amount of material used, the stupendous quantities of gasoline and oil that go to the fighting of battles of this kind; it gives us some idea of what the cost will be when we have to invade the continent of Europe with an army three or four or five times as large in order to bring victory to the united nations on the soil of Germany. And I am afraid we shall have to carry on that organization for years to come. We know we shall have to keep it up to a greater extent than we have done so far.
It seems to me we would be justified in using public money to help the Abasand Oil Company or any other company, although I do not think there is any other working there just now. We would be justified in constructing a

highway from Lac la Biche. There is a highway now from Edmonton to Lac la Biche- not a first-class highway, but it could be made first-class with a comparatively small expenditure, and it should be extended to Fort McMurray. The construction of a highway would be a very small expenditure, having regard to the great need for this oil. The hon. member for Davenport pointed out that we are paying hundreds of millions of dollars for importations of oil that we must have not only in time of war but at any time. As I said last summer, no nation will be great after this war or can take its rightful place in the field of advancement unless it has possession of this most vital of all requirements for this age of machinery, namely, oil and gasoline. The greatest supply not only in Canada but in the British empire is in that locality. I congratulate the minister on what he has achieved so far, although the hon. member for Davenport claims that he is the man who did it. I claim I had something to do with it also.
I did not claim that.

It was some forty years ago I was at Fort McMurray and Fort McKay. Some thirty years ago, when we had a little money, we hired geologists and men of experience and spent our own money in order to try to develop that field. Now the government is stepping in. I repeat that we should go to the extent of providing for construction of the highway. It would cost only a small percentage of the amount expended by the United States to build the Alaska highway in order to reach the battlefields of Asia, and the oil would be valuable hot only during the war but afterwards. Furthermore there is plenty of good land along that road once you reach House river, where soldiers could settle after the war if the highway were constructed.
I put this idea before the government to-dav because I am convinced that we should not be true to ourselves or show the confidence we ought to have in Canada if we do not go ahead now, when we have to tax people to the extent we do, in order to bring about the development of these vast resources. If the United States of America developed so fast in this line, as was mentioned yesterday by the hon. member for Calgary West, it is because they were not so much afraid as is the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar to let individual interests have their chance to make some money by developing the country's resources. In many states the oil rights and mineral rights belong to the owners of the soil, and that has induced more development
than any other thing we could do, by way of bonus or anything else. When oil possibilities were located by the geologists the big companies could not come along from abroad and go to the land office and file on the land and pay a few dollars to the man on top while they took millions out of the ground from the natural resources that belong to the people.
I said many times in the provincial house in Alberta that what we should have done there was to give the owners of the soil the title to the mineral rights. Up to 1890 when a man filed on a piece of land in Alberta or Saskatchewan he obtained the rights to the mineral under the land. Then that right was taken away, I do not know why, and the result was that development was retarded. It brought into the hands of a few the control of these resources and the poor farmer on top got nothing.
I believe the day will come when a great reservoir of gas and oil will be found between the great gas field at Medicine Hat, where more gas has gone into the air in the last half century than anywhere else in the world, up to the outcrop of tar sands hundreds of miles farther north. Somewhere between those points is a great reservoir of oil which some day will be found. I have an idea that the pool is somewhere in the country I live and that I represent. Be that as it may, if it were found there to-morrow the farmers and pioneers who went on that land and gave their best of soul and muscle to make that great land what it is now' would not benefit to the extent of a single dollar; it would go to some of the big companies while the men who own the topsoil can only stand and see the barrels rolling from their door and someone in Montreal or Toronto getting the benefit.
Hon. members will remember some years ago when Imperial Oil developed the great field at Fort Norman, where a pipeline is being constructed to deliver the oil to the Alaska highway. There was no possibility of bringing this oil dowm. The company came to Edmonton and asked for a pipeline charter. We all know what happened. The United Farmers of Alberta were then all-powerful, just a few months before they made a sweep of the then government; strong protest was made against the pipeline and the charter was not granted. There was no outlet for the oil until the great mineral development took place at Great Bear lake by the La Bines and other gold mining camps. I have great admiration for the initiative and enterprise and courage of these people. After the last war a number of us sent a man to Fort Norman

to file on some claims, in the hope that we who had been in Alberta all our lives might be able to do something to bring about the early development of these new resources.
I do not think I need say anything more. I am convinced that we would be fully justified in building a highway to Fort McMurray, and that we would be justified in spending a large amount of money on machinery for the separation of the oil and in proving this field. I know the Department of Mines and Resources has done its share. Last summer an engineer in this field sent me a sample of these tar sands. The engineers of the department who were working there said that in their experience there was nothing anywhere in the world finer than the tar sands which are found a few miles from Fort . McMurray. So that I say the government has done its share, and I am satisfied that we shall accomplish something. But as the member for that constituency, knowing the fight that has been carried on for many years to oring about the development of this great resource and to have a highway constructed,. I say there is no doubt that the best method of extracting sulphur is known already. I do not know who made the report which the minister read this afternoon, but I agree with the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar that this is no secret. It is known that it can be carried out without great cost, and that there is machinery which can be used to separate the oil from the sand. The only difficulty has been in getting sufficient money to instal this machinery on the scale necessary. Years ago one of the men who did a great deal in this connection, a young scientist from the university of Alberta, had one of these machines in operation. He showed it to a committee of the Alberta legislature, actually extracting oil from sand he had brought from McMurray. That machine did a thorough job; it extracted-all the oil, and the sand was left clear. The only problem was to ascertain whether this machine could be constructed id the size necessary in order to produce to the capacity required to make this a paying proposition in competition with other fields, or whether some changes would be needed before that could be done. So that I say we are justified in going ahead and spending money on this development. I am not much concerned as to how the government does it, as long as it is done.
I say to you, Mr. Chairman, and to the members of this committee that if we carry on this work now we shall reap the benefits long after the wounds of this war have been healed, as they will, God be thanked, be healed. The time will come when we shall not feel

so keenly our losses; when we shall no longer look with sorrow at the vacant places where dear ones used to sit; when we shall not feel so keenly the loss of those who gave their lives for this country. God always grants that these things do pass, though of course we shall always have remembrance in our hearts and souls for those who gave their lives in such a noble cause. We do not forget; we remember, but the deep sorrow passes away. After this is all over; when the storm clouds pass away; when the blood tinge that we now see everywhere in this world has vanished and the glorious sun shines on the land again, because of our great natural resources we shall be able to compete with anyone in the world. We have the initiative, the men, the materials, and everything else. This land is peopled by the descendants of the greatest and best human stock that God1 ever created. We have everything necessary to make Canada a great independent nation after the war, in what will be truly the great machine age. Therefore I say, let us develop these oil sands; let us bring them into production immediately, during the war, because we need oil so badly. No matter what happens to us in a political way, when our time comes to lay down the burden and let it be carried by someone better able to do so, at least we shall be able to say that we have done something really worth while for this country in addition to fighting a war.

Last evening I dealt with a number of things that I thought would be helpful in connection with the production of oil in Alberta. I wish now to refer to one matter that will not be helpful. speechtext: There is something to be said on the other side, too.

I must commend him for his attitude in this respect. In so doing I am not saying anything one way or the other with regard to the rest of his crown company objectives.
The minister made an attack on royalty companies, upon which I cannot compliment him. A share company, like a royalty company, must have acquired a lease before it can begin drilling. In acquiring that lease the lessor would retain the lessor's royalties. He would obtain the same royalty, in the case of a share company, as he would in the case of a royalty company. He would retain a gross royalty, in so far as that well is concerned.
Drilling in unproven structure is a highly speculative and honest venture. It costs no more to sell royalty shares than to sell shares in a share company. In fact it costs less to sell royalties than to sell shares in Calgary, because the pebple understand the royalty companies. They like those companies, and they will buy royalties more freely than they will shares.
They like them for two reasons in particular. In the first place the life of an oil well is from four to six years. If they invest in a share company they cannot, at the end of four or five years, go to the company and say, "I want my money back; here are my shares."

But in the case of a royalty company, when production is taken at the end of four or five years they get their money back, and they are through. They know definitely where they stand.
The second reason for their preference for royalty companies is, as I said last night, and I now repeat it, that no board of directors can divert that money to drilling for other oil wells, or divert it in any other speculative way. The realization of the well does not belong to the company, it belongs to the royalty holder. And no one but the royalty holder can reinvest it or deal with it.
For these reasons they prefer the buying of royalties to the buying of shares. I must point out further that no company can sell royalties in a royalty company or shares in a share company without first laying its plans before the public utilities commissioner, and receiving his consent. The public utilities commissioner is a quasi judicial official. It is his duty very carefully to check the contracts concerning royalties, or reserve shares for the entrepreneur. He checks up on the commissions paid on the sale of shares and on the sale of royalties. He must have a favourable report from a reputable geologist. He checks with meticulous care the plans of every company proposing to drill. In other words he is a most capable, efficient and painstaking official. I may say that I have appeared before him. on behalf of different companies, and I know whereof I speak. By his attack the minister has reflected upon this competent official, and it was also an attack upon our geologists and upon a number of royalty oil operators in Alberta. I suggest, to the minister that before he attacks the oil operators of Alberta or any other reputable class of citizens he should get correct information. Instead of going to the oil controller who is more than 1,000 miles away from the operations-I do not wish to cast any reflection upon the oil controller because he must get his information at second hand; the minister gets it at third hand or worse-he should go to this competent public utilities commissioner who knows his business. He would thus get his information at first hand. If he is too busy to go to Alberta, let him have this official come here. It would be a good thing if he came to Ottawa during the Easter holidays.
Let him have this official come here and arrange a conference with the Minister of Finance, Mr. Elliott, Doctor Eaton and the Minister of National Revenue. Let them all go into the matter and decide whether or not this official has been acting judicially in allowing these companies to sell shares and carry on business the way they are doing.

speechtext: What impressed me most was the statement that fifteen wells had been drilled by fifteen royalty companies in an unproven area and that thirteen had been abandoned. It struck me that that might seem to be a lack of economy and efficiency, particularly in time of war.

I do not say that I approve the drilling of all those wells, but they might just as well have been drilled by share companies as by royalty companies. The minister was attacking the royalty companies. In the land immediately to the south they got the biggest production ever obtained in any part of the Turner valley. There was then a rush into that particular area. While that rush may have been too great, I think if the matter were taken up with the official who passed on it, it would be shown that he was justified and that there was good reason for granting these permits.
In conclusion, let me again urge upon the Minister of Finance to grant to syndicates of small investors who may pool their capital to drill the right to offset the cost of drilling a dry hole against their individual income assessments. That would do a great deal to stimulate these highly speculative but honest ventures which are so essential to opening up of unproven areas. Without that stimulation I doubt if we are likely to discover many new oil wells. As I pointed out yesterday, it is the small operators who do the speculating. I also urge the minister to extendi the benefits of this resolution to wells already commenced, whether they were spudded-in on or before January 1, 1943.

I have just one or twc observations to make following the announcement by the Minister of Munitions and Supply in regard to crown companies. I was concerned about his culminating statement with respect to royalty companies having drilled some thirteen wells in the north end of the field which he said were failures.
I did not say they were failures; I said they had been abandoned.

That may be correct, but I should like to have more assurance than the mere statement that that is the situation. They may now have been closed temporarily, which is not an uncommon thing to happen. The continuation of drilling will probably depend upon the results obtained in some adjoining well on the structure. I believe that but for the finance resolutions and the taxing programme of this government a year ago, funds would have been available and some of these wells would have been sunk to the depth required to test the structure.
I have it as an opinion from a competent and reliable geologist that the northern end of that valley is still a potential oil field if the wells are sunk deep enough. Many of the wells have discontinued drilling at two, three and four thousand feet whereas the major production is obtained at seven, eight, nine and sometimes ten thousand feet. With all due deference, I do not think it is a correct statement to say that they have been abandoned.
Several of the wells were drilled to ten thousand feet, which is nearly two miles.

Ten thousand feet is not an exceptional depth in certain oil fields. They have gone much deeper than that in California; companies have gone back the second and third time to drill a well a little deeper. Look at the actual record. I shall take the Daily Oil Bulletin of March 10, 1943, and see whether the minister is justified in the statement he made with regard to oil royalty companies. First, I should like to quote what the minister said as reported on page 2141 of Hansard. He said:
A good deal has been said about the royalty companies. The lack of interest in royalty companies has been attributed to the government's taxation. I suggest that the lack of interest in royalty companies is due to the record of the royalty companies. They are peculiar to Alberta, and peculiarly to Turner valley. The royalty companies were started, I think, in 1939.
I have before me a list of the wells which I will give to the committee. Prior to 1938 there were five royalty companies drilling; in 1938 there were seven royalty company wells drilled; in 1939 there were eleven royalty wells drilled; in 1940 there were ten royalty

Because something is new or peculiar to a certain district, because something is out of the ordinary, something that has not been tried before, is it to be condemned? There is nothing sinister about a royalty company. In fact the royalty company grew out of, shall I say, the malpractices of share companies as such, because it was found that the people who bought shares in an oil company which brought in a well did not get what they thought they were getting. They did not get the production from the oil well -because the company used the money from the proceeds just as they saw fit and did not distribute the proceeds by way of dividends to the shareholders. In that way the financing of oil wells was discouraged, and it became difficult for an oil company to get a charter from the securities commissioner of Alberta until the system of royalty companies was set up.
A royalty company is really a misnomer. There is no such thing. There is a royalty agreement, and it ig this: The owners of certain leases deposit with a trust company a trust deed or agreement, including the lease. All the funds arising from the sale of royalties-the price at which the royalty shall be sold is fixed by the commissioner and the commission that shall be paid on the sale of that royalty is also fixed-go into the trust company and must be handled- under the trust agreement for no other purpose than to drill a well on a specific piece of property. The company or promoter as such has no control or jurisdiction and no right of disposal of the production derived from that well because, perforce, the trustee pays the drilling company on the certificate of the engineer. The trustee pays out the trust moneys in his hands. When production is found and the oil starts to come out, the pipeline company turns over a cheque direct to the gross royalty holders. Who are they? The crown in the right of the province and the owner of the lease. The owner of the lease gets from 10 to 124 per cent, or may get as high as 15 per cent. It may be recalled that last year in- this house my primary objection to the amendment to the Alberta resources agreement was that the province of Alberta was contemplating raising the royalty which it would take from any oil produced from any of the alienated oil lands. As I was saying, so much goes to the crown in the right of the province. It is the common and accepted practice, although it varies, that the owner of the lease shall get a gross royalty of 10 to 124 per cent. Throughout the United States 124-

Income War Tax
per cent is recognized. So that the gross royalty which was spoken of by the minister goes to the crown and the owner of the lease in the first instance; next comes the preferred royalty holder, who gets his out of the next production, until all his investment is paid back to him; then the deferred royalty holders come into the picture, and we have the commission brokers and those who have bought large blocks of preferred royalty interest. But the promoters and brokers do not get anything until the preferred royalty holder gets all his money back. The advantage of the royalty set-up of financing is that nobody can interfere with a person's one per cent, two per cent or ten per cent interest in the oil which comes out of that well; it cannot be diverted by any director or board of directors or management into some other field of exploration.
It would seem as though there were something terrible about a commission of twenty or twenty-five per cent for selling an interest in an oil well. I venture to say that in every province of the dominion twenty to twenty-five per cent is recognized as a fair commission for selling mining shares. It is not excessive. At least, it is known to and approved by the Ontario securities commission and by the securities commission of Alberta. So that there is nothing unhallowed, unfair or unconscionable in the royalty set-up as we have it at the present time.

. . . appointed a committee of experienced producers with headquarters at Calgary. This committee was made up of small operators-

-and representatives of the large oil companies.
I should like to know who the small operators were and who was speaking on their behalf. I do not know of any. The committee as advertised to the public in the press consisted of whom? Mr. McLeod, of the Royalite and Imperial Oil, a subsidiary of the Standard Oil of New Jersey; Mr. Galloway, of the Standard Oil of British Columbia, a subsidiary of the Standard Oil of California; Mr. Hunt, a representative of the McColl Frontenac and Texas corporation; Mr. Kemp, of the Alberta conservation board; and Mr. Brown, Jr., of the Brown Oil company, who organized many of the earlier royalty companies, the first major royalty company having
been organized by Mr. Brown's father, and who has lately undertaken some wildcat ventures with the Shell Oil company, which has no production in Canada. I am curious to know who was speaking on behalf of the independent companies, of the royalty companies, the pioneers of the oil industry in Alberta.
I would refer now if I may to the finance minister's amendments. I think the three changes which he announced last evening will be received with general appreciation and applause, particularly by those who are interested in the development of our oil resources. But I still believe that the crux of the problem is depletion allowances, and I should like a statement from the Minister of Finance as to why, having regard to the necessities of the case, we still retain that old 33^ per cent depletion allowance, when the United States of America in peace time and long after the oil industry had become a giant and well able to take care of itself, and despite repeated attempts to change it, still allow a depletion allowance of 27i per cent of the gross production up to a maximum of 50 per cent of the net production from any well; yet we start in and say, 33i per cent of the net and no more. "Depletion" is a confusing term, and the significance of it is not apparent unless you apply yourself to the problem. It is an allowance for a wasting or non-recurring asset; that is all. In other words, you allow one who goes out and produces to retain a certain portion of what he produces, free of tax.

I undertook to make a statement on this, but I have been questioned so much that I am in danger of losing the continuity of what I intended to say.
