Mr. McKINNON (Kenora-Rainy River)-Mr. Chairman, I approve this resolution except that in my opinion it does not go anywhere nearly far enough. It overlooks the prospector, one of the pioneers of our country who dowm through the years has gone out with a packsack on his back and has been respon- [DOT] sible for the mineral production in the mining areas throughout this country. I feel that he should have been given some consideration in this resolution.
I would also suggest that the resolution be extended to include gold mining companies.. While at the moment the government may not consider gold as essential, nevertheless it is-necessary for gold mining companies to be prospecting all the time if they want to be prepared to develop their properties further and keep their plant operating to capacity. In the district I have the honour to represent there is a large number of operating gold mining companies which pay a large amount of revenue to the dominion treasury. Around:
Income War Tax

these mining developments there have been built up through the years communities which in my opinion we should do * everything we can to encourage and assist. The gold mining industry will be one of the most important sources of employment after the war. We have a reconstruction committee of this house sitting now searching for ways and means of taking care of our people when they come back from the war and of those who may be out of employment when our war industries close down. There is no place that I know of where a finer opportunity exists for improvement than in the gold mining areas of this dominion, and I believe the minister will be well advised to extend these provisions to prospectors and gold mining companies.

The representation I intended to make has been put forward by the hon. member who has just taken his seat. If the government's desire is to encourage production of minerals, everything should be done to encourage prospectors and syndicates in exploration work. Is the resolution as now drafted restrictive in operation to companies heretofore incorporated, or will it apply to any companies which may be incorporated after this date whose purpose is to explore for base metals?
In this connection, I should mention the situation in Saskatchewan, where there are .great mineral possibilities, but where up to -the present time those engaged in this work have been unable to secure assistance from the joint fund provided by the United States iand Canadian governments to assure an ade-*quate production of base metals. There are [DOT]areas immediately north of Prince Albert, Saskatchewan, which contain great possibilities, but where up to the present no help has been available to those who over a period of years have continued the work of exploration for metals. In this connection I should like to hear from the Minister of Munitions and Supply. Saskatchewan has received very little in the way of war industry. Outside of one industry in Regina and one in Prince Albert, our industrial economy is much the same as it was before the outbreak of the war. If we are to build up a diversified economy-and we have resources available for the purpose-I bespeak assistance by the minister to those who have borne the brunt of the search for minerals up to the present time, so that the base metals which are there will be rendered available for the war effort, and when the war is over a further industry will have been in process of development.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The question asked by the hon. gentleman was whether the benefits of the resolution would extend to companies incorporated in the future. Is that correct?
That is right.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes; that is my understanding of the resolution. But I would point out that, if this resolution applies to mining companies, a new company would not be likely to have any income against which to write off the expenditure. It seems to me that the point is not an important one; it is almost academic, because the application is to companies which actually have income. It may be that a company incorporated in the future would gather up enough income in the course of a year or two to spend some of it in this form of activity. The resolution is designed to apply to existing mining companies, although I see no reason why it should not apply to future mining c companies.

I wish, briefly to support the statements of the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River. The Minister of Munitions and Supply knows, perhaps better than I do, the resources which lie at the head of * the lakes in the Thunder bay district. I have received many samples which, upon being tested, have been pronounced high grade ore by the department of .mines of Ontario. Many places where these deposits exist are waiting for the sort of assistance which the Minister of Mines and Resources provided for the haematite mine at Steep Rock. They jnst need the wherewithal to give them the "go" sign. As the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River said, we have resources in all kinds of metals which are well worth developing, and the ministers would be well advised to keep their eyes on that .part of Canada.

I should like first to endorse what was said by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River. To judge by the wording of this resolution, it would look very much as though prospectors, and groups of individuals not actually engaged in mining, are to get no assistance or relief from or by means of this resolution. The minister should tell us how those who really find these minerals will benefit from the exemptions which are provided under the resolution.
Another question I would ask is, to what extent the government is assisting in the production of those essential minerals which are already known to exist in commercial quantities?

Income War Tax
A booklet published by the Department of Mines and Resources and the Department of Munitions and Supply, entitled "The Industrial Front," tells us, for instance, that the Canadian output of aluminum has increased many-fold during the war, that we are now producing more than the total production of the rest of the world in 1939, and that the Aluminum Company of Canada is producing forty per cent of the supplies used by the united nations. Then we learn that the principal requirements for the making of aluminum in Canada are, bauxite from the tropics of South America- British Guiana, I understand-cryolite from the arctic expanses of Greenland, acid-grade fluorspar from the United States; and the contribution which Canada makes is the electric power from the rivers of Quebec. In other words, every pound of raw material which goes into the millions of pounds of aluminum produced in this country is imported. Notwithstanding the shipping necessities of the present time, and notwithstanding the fact that numerous railway sidings all across this country are blocked with the products of our factories now needed at the front, we are still using valuable shipping space to bring in from South America every pound of the raw' material that goes to the making of this aluminum. In contrast with that I w'ish to read an excerpt from the Northern Miner of April 1, 1943, page 20:
The United States bureau of mines is speeding up the development of alumina-bearing earth materials and low grade bauxite in an effort to render the country independent of foreign sources of raw material for production of aluminum. A grant of $500,000 has been given by congress to this end and seven laboratories and pilot plants have been assigned to the work. . . .
Canada has a potential source of alumina in the extensive deposits of nepheline syenite, and experiments already conducted have indicated commercial success on a production basis. Nothing is being done to further this project, as Ottawa has refused priorities for the necessary plant construction material.
In the light of the facts that I have stated regarding the importation of raw material and the fact that it is well known that at Lakefield and on the north shore of lake Superior there are literally mountains of this aluminabearing material, and it is generally known that there is a process fairly well perfected by which aluminum can be produced from this nepheline syenite, the only reason I can see why we are not taking steps to use that material is in the first place that the bauxite from British Guiana has a little higher percentage of alumina and, second, that it can be mined there with native labour and brought to this country so that a greater profit can be
made from the manufacture of the finished product by the aluminum trust. We are entitled to some explanation as to whether any steps are being taken to produce aluminum from the raw material that exists in this country.
A second metal to which I wish to refer briefly is cobalt. To-day, notwithstanding the abundance of cobalt-bearing ore in Ontario, we are bringing the material from which cobalt is made, a residue from copper mining, from Rhodesia and hauling it to Hastings in Ontario and Niagara Falls, refining it there and shipping it back to England. Canadian-produced cobalt ore, cobalt produced in the Cobalt camp, where there is an. abundance of ore left over as a residue of the silver mining that took place years ago when cobalt was a drug on the market, is being stock-piled far the United States government. I have a return which shows that at the time the Deloro Smelting company which, owns the only smelter in this country for the smelting of cobalt, made an agreement with the British government to process quantities of Rhodesian cobalt, they had on hand 636,385 pounds of' cobalt partly processed from Canadian material, when the plant changed its method of processing in order to process the ore brought in from Rhodesia.
There- is a great deal of questioning being done by those interested in the production of cobalt in Ontario. They are handicapped, first, because the only mill in the camp is, I understand, an old one, thirty years of age, that formerly belonged to the O'Brien interests, the same interests that now own, I believe, the Deloro smelting plant, It is now owned and operated, I am told, by a formeT employee of the O'Brien interests. Producers in that camp tell me that the charge for milling is exorbitant, that recovery is very low, and that they are being cheated out of much of the value of their ore. That ore contains a considerable amount of silver; but only silver running more than fifty ounces to the ton is paid for; nickel is paid for only when it runs more than five per cent, and then it is only paid for at 5J cents a pound, while the market price is 35 cents. The cobalt ore is fairly rich in arsenic, but no return is made to the producer for the arsenic. In other words,- the producers in that camp believe that they are being held up by the one mill which is operating. They are being further held up by the one smelter, owned by the Deloro or O'Brien interest.
Attempts have been made to interest United States capital. I have seen correspondence
Income War Tax

which would indicate that United States capital was prepared to invest in an additional milling and smelting plant in Cobalt had it, been possible to get the approval of the metals controller. That correspondence would indicate that it was impossible to get that approval.
While that situation is developing in Cobalt, I find, according to a return I have, that cobalt is being mined north of Kenora, at Wemer lake, Ontario, away in from the railroads. Some four hundred tons of cobalt have been flown out of that camp and sold to United States interests. At the present time, according to the return, a mill is being flown into that camp. What is interesting to me is that the person interested in the Werner lake affair is the adviser to the metals controller.
I think I should say there is no government money invested in that mill.
I did not say there was.

It is entirely a private
matter. I suggest to the hon. member that when he names a man, and names an interest, he should make it perfectly clear that the man is not using his interest to obtain any government intervention.
_ Mr. NOSEWORTHY:	The point I am
interested in is that the cobalt producers in Cobalt have been finding it extremely difficult to produce, mill and refine Canadian-produced cobalt, while the smelter at Deloro is treating ore brought all the way from Rhodesia. I have a pamphlet called "Metal and Mineral Markets", which is a weekly news service published by the Engineering and Mining Journal, in which I find an article dated November 14, 1935, as follows:
The Association of German Cobalt Producers and the Cobalt Association, consisting of Union Miniere du Haut-Katanga, Deloro Smelting and Refining Company,-
That is the one in Ontario.
-Rhokana Corporation, and Miniere de Bou-Azzer et du Craara (Morocco) have signed a trade pact on the marketing of cobalt and cobalt salts, according to S. B. Redecker, United States consul at Frankfort-on-Main.
Back in 1935 it was stated:
The pact is hailed with enthusiasm in German metal circles, for the reason that it takes into consideration Germany's difficult foreign exchange situation by giving preference to the importation into Germany of ore rather than finished metal or intermediate materials; is designed to improve the position of German producers, as well as foreign, in striving for a gradual improvement of prices; and guarantees an adequate supply of cobalt indispensable for German needs. The pact, moreover, gives Ger-
IMr. Noseworthy.]
man producers entire freedom in the utilization of cobalt raw materials of domestic origin as well as foreign materials in which the cobalt content is very small or less than one per cent, to the working of which German smelters have long been accustomed.
Previously existing foreign agreements regarding cobalt ores and residues have been assimilated into the new pact with Germany, and an understanding concerning finished cobalt metal. Provision is also made for an export quota for German cobalt manufactures corresponding to the average relation in recent years of German exports to the sales of the foreign members of the pact.
The question I placed upon the order paper asked whether the government had knowledge of the fact that the Deloro Smelting company was, prior to the war and I understand until about 1939 or 1940, a member of the international cobalt cartel. Apparently the government had no knowledge of that fact.
I would ask the minister to consider these facts together. Here we have what is definitely a retardation of the production of cobalt, a vital mineral. The amount of cobalt required and its uses, as set out in the minister's own booklet, will indicate that it is an essential war mineral. We have a retardation of the production of cobalt in northern Ontario, where it exists in abundance. We are bringing it from mines in Rhodesia, owned by one member of that international cobalt trust, all the way to Ontario, where it is smelted in a plant that belongs to another member of that international cobalt trust, and we then ship the finished product back to England. All the while our own Canadian-produced cobalt has been stock-piled without having been used for war purposes at all. Producers in Cobalt are being handicapped severely in the production of this mineral and, I am told by a member, get no support or encouragement whatever from the controller of metals or the government for the development of their industry. I should like the minister to give us an explanation.

I have listened with interest to what the hon. member for York South has told us about aluminum and cobalt. As for aluminum, it is true that the raw materials, the bauxite, the cryolite and the flux material, are not of Canadian origin. However, I doubt if that is a source of weakness to Canada's interest in the industry', for at least it is not depleting our raw materials. The only Canadian element they' use at all is the water that runs down the river in any event, and with that small drain on our natural resources we have a tremendous industry which is a great employer of labour and a great buyer of manufactured commodities.

Income War Tax
The hon. member suggests that possibly a source of the raw material could be found in Canada. It is true, I believe, that about one-sixth of the earth's surface contains alumina, but it is a question of the concentration. The richest form in which alumina is found is in the bauxite of South and Central America. The Canadian company owns extensive deposits in British Guiana and has recently opened up other deposits in Jamaica. That happens to be the cheapest raw product that can be obtained. It is true that there is bauxite in Arkansas which, while it is a much lower grade than the central American bauxite, is probably the highest concentration to be found on this continent. We have deposits in Canada that could be used, at a cost. That possibility has been explored thoroughly; experiments have been made in the laboratories of the aluminum plant and in the research laboratories at Ottawa. If the worst came to the worst we could, at a very large capital expenditure, obtain the alumina element in this country. It is all a matter of cost. Canada is a very large user of aluminum at the moment, and naturally it is to the advantage of Canada to have a low-cost product here. If Canada wishes to maintain the industry at anything like its present scale, it is necessary that the Canadian industry shall sell its product in world markets at world competitive costs. Therefore it is necessary, if the Canadian company is to maintain its position, that it obtain its raw products in the lowest cost market, and I see nothing detrimental to the Canadian economy in that. I may say that the aluminum industry is a privately-owned industry. The Canadian government has no investment in it whatsoever. We were very fortunate to have that industry in Canada. I gave the story of it the other day, and pointed out the contribution it is making to the war effort of the allies. It is an industry of which Canada may be immensely proud.
Canada is a producer of cobalt. It happens that North Africa produces cobalt ore as a byproduct from other operations, and from that country ore is immensely cheaper than the Canadian product, so much so in fact that it can be shipped from North Africa to Canada, smelted in Canada, and sent on to the consuming markets at a lower cost than the similar product made from ore mined in Canada. There is nothing much Canada can do about that situation. Perhaps it could close down the smelter. The smelter is privately owned. We could close the industry, or we could say that we refuse to handle north African ore. But the only result would be that north
African ore would be smelted elsewhere, and our product would continue to be a drug on the market.
My hon. friend says the department has taken no interest in the cobalt ore. I tell him that if my department had not taken an active interest in cobalt ore mining operations would have stopped some years ago. Very early in the war the government financed a stock pile of that ore. Later on, our metals controller persuaded an agency of the United States government to pay considerably more than the price at which north African ore could be imported, in order to continue and increase the stock pile. As a result of those efforts the miners in the Cobalt area have been able to find a market for their product.
My hon. friend makes a great point of Deloro's being included in a cartel. He says he is speaking for the miners in the Cobalt area. Whether the cartel exists to-day or not, I cannot say, but, if so, I do not know whether that would be detrimental. As I understand it. the purpose of a cartel is to hold up the price of a product. The higher the price of the product, the greater the chance the cobalt miners have to receive a higher price for their product. Therefore, whether a cartel exists or not, I suggest he did not make his point that the result of the cartel is detrimental to the interests of the miners in the Cobalt area.
The hon. member says that a building permit for a plant to develop alumina from Canadian raw materials was refused. I say that no application has been made. My department, and the government as a whole, has taken an active interest in investigating the possibilities of obtaining raw materials in Canada. Had the companies shown any desire to make the investment required to use Canadian raw materials we would certainly have cooperated fully.
Similarly, in the Cobalt area, if anyone wishes to build a smelter to smelt Canadian cobalt ores, in line with the property which he mentioned and in which he said an adviser in my department is interested, my department will give that man any and every assistance. But no one has come forward who wishes to undertake such a project. I do not think I can add anything further at this time.

I have one or two suggestions in connection with an extension of the provisions of resolution 19. I have put the suggestions before the Minister of National Revenue, in a written memorandum.
Before dealing with them, however, I should like briefly to pay tribute to the foresight and good judgment of the Minister of Finance, the Minister of Munitions and Supply and the Minister of National Revenue in the vision
Income Tl'ar Tax

they had a year ago when they included from British Columbia to Nova Scotia for the
section 10A in the Income War Tax Act, which is chapter 28 of last year's statutes. The committee will recall that provision is there made for a forty per cent exemption for contributions to syndicates or mining partnerships organized for prospecting in Canada for base metals or strategic minerals, and then there were placed certain limitations on the amount which any one man might invest, and obtain his forty per cent exemption.
There was also a provision made last year for a similar exemption for amounts actually expended by a mining or exploration company in prospecting for those two types of metals. While I would not say they have been entirely due to that legislation, the fact is that the results obtained in Canada in the last fourteen months in the matter of important discoveries and contributions to the war by way of strategic materials is almost a romance.
I shall trouble the committee with only four examples, stating them as briefly as I can. I take these examples from our official handbook for 1943 issued only last week by the government. At page 96 under the heading "Mines and Minerals" we find these four items recorded. Undoubtedly the Department of Mines and Resources was consulted when this part of the handbook was edited. It states:
The demand for metals of all kinds increases rapidly in war time, and Canada soon found deficiencies in the supplies of magnesium, tungsten, molybdenum. . . . Ores of most of these metals were known to exist, and mining companies and prospectors assisted by officers of the mines departments of the dominion and provincial governments immediately commenced a reprospecting of old ground, and the search for new, promising geological territory.
Then, it deals with magnesium in this way:
Perhaps the most outstanding achievement during the present war in the production of strategic metals is the manufacture of magnesium. ... In the new plant of Dominion Magnesium Limited, near Renfrew, Ontario-
About fifty miles from this chamber.
-a method developed at the national research council uses dolomite as the raw material.
That plant has revolutionized the production in Canada of magnesium, a strategic war material.
Then at page 98 we find this reference to tungsten:
Canada's very important place in the manufacture of war equipment created an unprecedented demand for tungsten. Tungsten alloy steels are extensively used in making armour plate and armour-piercing projectiles.
Skipping a bit, we find the following:
Geologists from government departments and from private companies have been in the field 
past year and a half searching for tungsten ores and their efforts have not gone unrewarded. A very important discovery has been made in British Columbia which will be operated as a government enterprise.
Mercury is referred to on page 99 as follows:
Prior to the present war, practically all of Canada's mercury requirements were imported, but a mercury deposit has been brought into production at Pinchi lake. British Columbia, which can more than supply the needs of this country.
The next mineral dealt with is something of which I have personal knowledge. I acted for the widow of the unfortunate young prospector who made a mica discovery near Mattawa in Ontario and who lost his life in an accident a few months after. The report on mica is as follows:
Among the non-metallic minerals, mica, graphite, fluorspar and magnesite might be considered the most strategic. Mica finds its greatest use as an insulator in the making of electrical equipment. . . . An extremely important deposit of white mica has been discovered near Mattawa, Ontario, and is now in production.
I had the privilege of attending a conference with engineers from the United States who have advised the largest producers of mica in that country. They believe that in the discovery near Mattawa we have the greatest mica deposit in the world. I shall not spend any more time with these strategic minerals. With our wonderful production of munitions and raw materials which is expanding all the time and will expand under this legislation we bid fair to become the arsenal of the empire as in the past we became the granary of the empire. I understand from the minister that my memorandum will perhaps be acceptable, so that I shall not labour it.
Resolution 19 refers to all companies mining metalliferous and strategic minerals, but it does not cover the exploring for such minerals. I have suggested that we should add the exploration companies as well as syndicates and mining partnerships. We would then be giving encouragement to the small fellow. This point was raised this afternoon in connection with oil, and it can be raised much more powerfully with regard to mining. I had the privilege of spending ten years in the mining camps of northern Ontario and knowing intimately the prospector and his bravery, fortitude and courage, and the hardships which he has to endure. If the larger companies are to be given this exemption in connection with exploration costs, we should include the smaller exploration company and the syndicate and the

Income War Tax
prospector himself. I ask the minister and his advisers to consider this matter, which has been brought up already by one of my hon. friends.
I wish strongly to support the suggestion made by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. McKinnon) that exploration for gold should be included in the exemption. The committee will realize that a gold mining company, which is a company mining metalliferous minerals, which prospects for base metals or strategic materials can secure an exemption on such costs. This resolution does not provide any exemption for the expenses of prospecting for gold. My experience of years ago and such intimacy as I have had with the industry since has shown me beyond per-adventure that it is not the great corporation or the great mining operating company which makes the original discovery; it is the prospector, supported quite frequently by a few of his friends or by a small mining syndicate. I have been in many of them in days gone by. You lose eight out of ten times, but if you strike it once you may be rewarded. It has been the little fellow, the man of small means, who has made this country noted as the most powerful mineral producing country in the world.
I should like to submit for the consideration of the minister one or two reasons why gold prospecting should be included. Prospecting for gold has become almost non-existent in the last five or six or seven years. I do not ask the committee to take my word for that. I should like hon. members to bear with me for a moment while I quote an authority which I feel sure the two ministers who are present will commend as being one that should be listened to. Doctor R. C. Wallace is the head of Queen's university where there is a very important science and mining school. He has been engaged for the past year and a half on what has been known as the James committee under Doctor James. With the aid of the department of mines he has given special attention to this problem of prospecting and the danger of prospecting drying up. I should like to quote from the report of the proceedings of the special committee on reconstruction and reestablishment before which Doctor Wallace appeared. I quote first from page 105 of the proceedings, as follows:
With regard to mining, there too we have very full data material, and there are two problems in mining which I might simply outline.
I am not going to go into those two problems because it is not necessary to do so. I commend to the department the language which appears on page 106.

I do not wish to interrupt the hon. gentleman, but I understand it is against the rules of the house to quote from a report of a committee which is at present sitting. The hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) was stopped from doing this a few days ago.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: If the committee has not brought in a report covering the matter mentioned by the hon. member, it would be out of order.

I am not quoting the report of the committee; I am quoting the evidence given by Doctor Wallace before the committee.
I shall not be long, and I think it would be helpful if we had this before us.
I am only asking that the rules be applied impartially. If my hon. friend is allowed to read this to-night, that is all right, but if I wish to read something tomorrow I do not want to be stopped.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I have already given my decision that it is out of order to quote any part of a report which a committee that is at present sitting may make.

Let me say then, without quoting any express language from Doctor Wallace, that he has been engaged by this government to investigate this very important question, and as a result of his investigation, to sum it up, he has reached the conclusion that the danger is, as he would put it, that we are in a lower level of employment in mining than the normal one when the war is over. He puts it that the training of men as prospectors is very important. He puts it that a great number of the new discoveries to be made in Canada are under clay, and not on bare rock and that that training needs ito be given. I must not use his exact language; I am trying to paraphrase the effect of what he has told us. He puts it that there is practically no incentive to invest money in. mining enterprise to-day, that it is a very ticklish and speculative business-I do not think we need an eminent man like Doctor Wallace to tell us that.
But here is the danger, that if we let prospecting for gold dry up or if we fail to encourage it, then as soon as peace, which we all hope will shortly be declared, comes, we shall have a tremendous need for goods and foreign exchange, in order to continue our pre-war purchases from the United States. The committee will remember that two years ago the then Minister of Finance- I think it was in the regime of Mr. Ralston-

Income War Tax

met with the gold mining industry and urged them in the strongest possible way to increase the production of gold, because it was then thought essential that we should dlo so in order to have sufficient foreign exchange to buy the- goods we needed. The gold mining companies responded in varying degrees. They increased, their plants and their expenditures and: increased the production of gold. More recently-the Minister of Finance himself knows better than I as to this-the generous policy of the United States toward us has, I believe, enabled us to secure the goods we require for war purposes without our having to pay for them on the barrelhead with foreign, exchange or even with products of our owTn for what we get from them. Therefore the minister might properly tell us that the need of to-day for gold as a medium of foreign exchange is not so great as it was heretofore. But I venture to predict this, that at the conclusion of the war the generous policy of the United States toward us will of necessity cease, and from the conclusion of the peace treaty onwards we shall be expected to pay that country either in goods or in gold' for our annual requirements from it, such as anthracite, cotton, corn, iron ore and half a dozen other commodities for which we are largely dependent upon our good neighbours to the south.
If that be so, the .policy of permitting the prospector to disappear or of failing to take all reasonable measures to secure new discoveries of gold is a policy that in my submission would be an improper one for us to follow. From the time a prospector makes a discovery, no matter how rich or important it may be, one cannot count on any production for a period of at least three years, and if we have a short-sighted policy in this regard we might find, when the war ends, that we have overlooked one of the easiest methods of providing work, and foreign exchange with which to .purchase our requirements. I venture to say that the expenditures under these exemptions would not be great and that the loss of taxes owing to the amendment of last year has not cost the finance department $2,000,000. The encouragement to the individual prospector and the encouragement to prospect for gold should undoubtedly be continued1.
The amendment necessary to this resolution would be very simple. All that the minister would' have to do would .be to add before the word "base" in the third line the two words, "metalliferous ores", so that it would read "their exploration expenditures

incurred in searching for metalliferous ores, base metals and strategic materials," and so on. It is as simple as that in language, but it involves a matter and a problem of major importance, and I commend it to the consideration of the ministers who have to do with it.
Mr. MaeINNIS: I should like to ask the hon. member for Parry Sound a question. I understand that it is not the policy of the government at the present time to encourage gold mining. I think that certain actions which were taken during the last year or two by the government have been to discourage gold mining. What would be the object of encouraging gold prospecting and discouraging gold mining?

I shall be very happy to answer that. 1 think the explanation is one that it is not difficult to apprehend. It is this. The policy of the government has not been to discourage gold mining but the result of the policy of the government, its call for manpower-there are splendid young men in all our mines as the hon. member for Cape Breton South and the hon. member for Vancouver East know-forced as we have been to interfere more or less with all industries, found a very ready response from the type of men, skilled miners, to be found in the gold mines. In the first year and a half of the war the recruiting results in the gold mining camps were remarkable. They denuded the gold mines of the necessary labour to keep up their production, and I would say that they are running at practically only two-thirds of their peace-time production to-day, due entirely to the scarcity of skilled labour, caused entirely by the contribution to the war made by the employees in the mines, many of whom are overseas to-day. While that is a most creditable result, it was not'something done to discourage gold mining. Let me point out this to my hon. friend, and it is apropos of his question. I do not wish to go into the matter too deeply, but let us say that one-third of the skilled miners in this country are now away from the mines and in the armed forces. What will happen to them when they come back from this war? We have to think now of absorbing them into industry, and if we stop making gold discoveries-and it must be remembered that our present mines are necessarily depleting their gold reserves, because a mine has only a given life and it is not too long-it does seem to me that we should be failing in this way to make provision for absorbing a great many of our young men who are trained in mining and

many others who would enter that wonderful calling when they come back from the war. Since it would help to solve that unemployment problem which we all recognize, that in itself is an argument in favour of prospecting for gold.
-My hon. friend made a very good1 argument but did not answer my question at all. I can well understand how he can win cases in court if one does not pay close attention to him.
I am very sorry. What was the question?

Why should the government discourage gold mining or the use of man-power in gold mining and at the same time encourage prospecting for gold? My hon. friend did not say anything about the government's policy of withdrawing men from gold mining.

No. no.
-and I told my hon. friend that the government did not discourage the gold mining industry.

I had not intended to hold up the proceedings at this time. The hon. member for Parry Sound and the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River have gone over what I should have liked to say. However, having the honour of representing some of the largest gold mines in Canada, I feel that I have the right to say a few words here. I have lived in that part of the country for forty-one years. I believe I know every prospector and how every one of those claims was staked. In my
riding are twelve gold mines producing and paying dividends. Within two miles in the township of Teck there are seven, and not' one of those was staked by a mining company.
I could give the committee the name of every man that staked each mine. I know who staked the Hollinger, the McIntyre and the Noranda.
An hon. member was insisting that there is no point in looking for gold1 or starting new gold mines. When Noranda was staked, it was staked for a gold mine, and what has it turned out to be? That brings out the point that when you are out looking for minerals you never know what you will find. Noranda found, after mining some time, that they had a copper mine, and they are now producing great quantities of copper for our war effort. Kamascotia is another example; I believe the government have had something to do with it. The Hollinger gold mine is undertaking part of that work. I believe there is a lot of copper up in that district; that remains to be seen. At any rate it has been staked by syndicates. I believe the minister would do well, as the hon. member for Parry Sound has already pointed out, to allow syndicates and exploration parties the same opportunity that he has given to the mining companies. That is all they are asking for; if they receive the same privileges which are accorded to mining companies they will be well satisfied.
The prospector should have consideration. I have watched prospectors, big strong fellows, go out and after six weeks come back all flybitten and thin. No one knows what these men go through to find the minerals which we have found in that section of the country. As the hon. member for Parry Sound remarked, what are you to do when these men come back from the war? I believe Kirkland Lake provided as many recruits for its size as any town in the country. The reason for that is that every man who works underground is fit; he must be fit before he can do that work.
I believe the minister would be well advised to accept the suggestion which has been made in this connection.

I was rather astonished at
the remarks of the hon. member for Parry' Sound. I believe, and I hope the majority of hon, members agree with me, that- the production of gold during the war cannot help in any shape or form our war effort, namely, the war effort of the joint allied nations.
Whether the production of gold will be of any value to this country after the war is, of course, another matter. But take the postwar period. It will not be necessary to have
Income War Tax

gold as a backing against our currency internally. Both the governor of the Bank of Canada and Doctor Cyril James have admitted that. So far as our internal currency is concerned there is no need of a metallic backing. On the other hand, if it is argued that gold will be needed to settle an unfavourable balance of trade, I ask, is there any reason to believe that Canada after the war will have with any nation an unfavourable balance of trade? I would think our main difficulty after the war will be that, as a result of our favourable balance of trade, other nations will find the greatest difficulty in shipping us a sufficient quantity of goods to maintain an even balance. I cannot visualize Canada having any difficulty in paying by the exportation of goods for any imports she may require after the war; and if we do not need gold after the war to pay off an unfavourable balance of trade, of what possible advantage can it be to this country to expand its production?
At the present time we are able to export in the neighbourhood of $200,000,000 worth of gold. Surely that will be ample to meet any unfavourable balance of trade which we may have with any part of the world. Our great difficulty after this war will be to find markets. We shall have to accept imports in return for exports, and it is only further complicating the problem to increase the production of gold in order to increase our exports, because when you increase your exports you also have to increase your imports. I can see no justification for utilizing labour at this time to prospect for gold, when w'e are already in a position to produce far more gold than we require.
If this country were poor as regards the production of other forms of wealth; if we had a shortage of agricultural products or of manufactures, it might be desirable to increase our production of gold so that we could receive more imports. But would any hon. member suggest for one minute that Canada after this war will not be in a position to produce enough goods to pay for all the imports we want? Unless it can be shown that we cannot do so, there can be no justification for wasting labour at this time to find ways and means of producing more gold after this war.

Would the Minister of Munitions and Supply give me a little further information regarding a statement he made? He told me that if we did not smelt imported cobalt in Canada it would be smelted elsewhere and Canadian cobalt would remain a drug on the market. Does the minister not know that the production of cobalt in Canada last year was the lowest it has been since
(Mr. Queldh l	.
1931; that it was only half the amount mined ini Canada in 1936; that the price of cobalt is fixed by an international cartel and to-day there is a world price in cobalt; that the Canadian producer has to sell his cobalt at the same price as the south African? I wonder who is getting the benefit of the cheaper production from South Africa. Is it the British government, or the company which mines it, or the company that is smelting? Is not the fact that the company which is mining this ore and the company which is smelting it in Canada are members of the same international cartel, the determining factor in this situation? Is not that the fact which determines why we are smelting this imported ore in Canada, and leaving our own ore on the stock pile?

I am not very close to this situation. I see these things pass through; I give the facts as I remember them. Deloro always was a customs smelter; that is, it buys ore and sells the product. There is a world price for cobalt. I dare say it is fixed by the cartel, as is the world price for a good many metals. I suppose the spread between the cost of the ore at the smelter and the selling price of the product determines the profit. Deloro did use a certain small amount of cobalt to meet a very limited demand before the war. I suppose they did find that they could bring in ore in shiploads cheaper than the Canadian product. Canada is a very small user of cobalt, and therefore we are not greatly concerned with the market price. We buy in the open market as we require it. But my comment about the cartel was that if the price were lower it would be that much more difficult for the Canadian producers to carry on. I repeat that we have financed a stock pile of cobalt here beyond our immediate needs. We also arranged with our friends across the line to stock-pile a further amount, so that we now have, I think, more cobalt in stock than we have ever had before, and by that means we have kept the industry about normal.

I find myself in almost complete agreement with what the hon. member for Parry Sound has just said. I would go even further than he suggested in the matter of tax reduction for prospectors. During a war economy many unsound practices occur in the mining industry. These practices may be both financial and engineering. If it had not been for the war, prospecting for such metals as tungsten, molybdenum,' mercury and chromium oxide would probably not have been encouraged. I think the government is to be commended for having encouraged them.

These are strategic metals, absolutely essential for the carrying on of hostilities. They are war metals. But-and this is the point-when we come back to a peace-time economy we shall probably find that many of these deposits which the government is working or in different ways assisting private industry to work-Wartime Metals I believe is the company-are not commercially workable; in other words, they do not pay because in other parts of the world there are larger, richer and more easily worked deposits which now, owing to the war or to enemy occupation, are denied to us. When the war is over, these deposits will again become available to us. What I suggest to the minister is that allowance should be made up to 100 per cent for the work done to bring these deposits of strategic minerals into production. I believe such undertakings should be treated in exactly the same way as the oil producing companies are treated. I think the case for these companies is even stronger, because I'do not think anyone would deny that, after the war,'oil, no matter where you get it, will be salable, a valuable commodity. But many mineral deposits that we are necessarily opening up now will not be economically workable when the peace comes.
Another and even more important point that I do not believe hon. members fully appreciate is the dire strait Canada is in at the present time on account of the lack of the development of new metal deposits in the last ten or fifteen years. The deposits we have developed of chromite, mica, magnesium and other metals of which the hon. member for Parry Sound spoke are emergency operations. I believe a very good case can be made out that in the main these are not economic developments. But I am speaking of our chief base metals, copper, lead, zinc, nickel. I am not including aluminum, because it is not mined in any great volume in Canada. But of those four strategic metals in the production of which we as a nation excel there have been no major discoveries, I think I am safe in saying, since the discovery of Noranda in 1927. A mining industry cannot flourish unless discoveries are being made all the time; that is almost axiomatic. We have not done that. We have not done it because of our taxation policy. I disagree with our taxation policy on the development of metals, and that includes the previous administration as well as this one.
The discovery and mining of mineral deposits are as hazardous as, or even more hazardous than, prospecting and drilling for oil, the difference being that for oil you drill your hole and if it is a "duster", if it is
dry, everything is gone, you are out your original stake. But in mining, you start off and get teased along; the vein looks good; the diamond drilling shows good values over narrow widths. You put up more money, sink a shaft, put in a little plant, develop one or two levels. It still looks good. You continue to put up more money, and by the time you develop the property to four or five hundred feet you find that you have spent three or four times your original stake. Then the ore pinches out, and you have nothing. Our policy of taxation has been that if you lost money, that was just too bad; but if you made a mine, immediately you were taxed. You were not allowed any deduction for the work you had done or the money you had invested in prospecting. The net result has *been that prospecting has virtually died on our hands. The individual prospector, the small syndicate, the man who knows the bush, has not been able to get a grub-stake. He has languished in unemployment, and the country has gone undeveloped. That is a situation the seriousness of which cannot possibly be over emphasized. We have to continue with the development of our metal resources'..
The main mines in Canada-I will mention them: International Nickel, Noranda. Consolidated Smelter and Hudson Bay, not to mention the smaller ones-have done everything possible since the war to increase production. They have had just one goal ahead of them-to increase production and get the. metal overseas. The result has been that1 unsound practices have been followed in connection with several of these properties in order to obtain the maximum production of metal. In some instances the mines have' been high-graded. By that I mean the rich ore has been mined at a far greater rate than it would have been under a normal economy, and you have a great deal of low grade ore remaining in the mines that normally would have been taken out. Once you mine a vein or a stope and go by, you can never go back and get what you have left. That is lost to the country for all time. That is what we are doing; that is what we have had to do in order to obtain greater production, and that makes it even more important that we should encourage in every possible way prospectors, individuals, mining companies, speculators or whatever you want to call them; we should encourage money to go into prospecting in order to develop the mineral resources of this country.
The suggestions made by Principal Wallace have been summarized in the press, and L

1.	That the relatively short life of a mine requires heavy total investment, which calls for a substantial return.
2.	War-time conditions have thrust gold mining into the background, with the result that no new properties are coming up and the post-war employment possibilities of the base

3.	The present rates of taxation are not only discouraging financial investment in mining, but they are also lowering the actual amount of available ore that can be mined. That was my second point to-night.

6.	Canada's surplus of electric power after the war may enable our entry into the ferroalloy industry on a very important scale. That is particularly important when we think of the possible shift to aluminum. We are passing into the age of light metals and alloys. We shall find that magnesium, aluminum, tungsten and other light alloys will be the metals of the future.
And lithium.

Yes; lithium is another. We shall find that the motorcar of the future, for instance, will be a great deal lighter and easier to propel; that our motive-power engines will be smaller and more efficient. The use of light metals will become paramount. To fit ourselves for the future, the production of these new light metals must be encouraged, and the government must encourage them now. We cannot afford in the future to allow other countries to usurp our rightful place in the metallurgical life of the world.
I had not intended to say anything about gold, but I cannot allow the statements that have been made to go quite unchallenged. Gold is now and will be in future a vital metal, an important sinew of war and peace. As the minister well understands, from now on, until some type of stabilization occurs, we shall find ourselves faced with an extremely dangerous inflationary period. And we shall find ourselves facing the necessity of having the ,
people of this continent trusting paper money. We shall have to show that we have gold coverage, not only for our paper money but for the bonds we are to issue in great volume very soon, and probably on several more occasions before peace comes.
That is why we need gold internally. After all, when the banks closed their doors in 1933, during the panic in the United States, what was it the United States people wanted-although they did not realize it? Why was there a run on the banks? They wanted their money; they wanted gold. We shall need gold coverage. The history of the world has shown that to occur after every war and after every revolution-and we are in a revolution now, whether we realize it or not. We shall need gold, from now on, just as much as we needed it for United States exchange, when the United States was a neutral country.
I agree with the hon. member for Parry Sound that encouragement should be given to gold prospecting, not only for the reasons I have already stated but for those suggested by the hon. member for Timiskaming. When one goes prospecting -and Noranda is the historic example-he looks for a certain metal, and he may find almost anything. Under our extremely complicated geological formations, and the extreme complications in the formation of the pre-cambrian shield, we may find anything. It has frequently been found that goldbearing ore will contain many other important metals.
The three major united nations, namely, Russia, the United States and the British empire, are all primary gold producers. In fact, among them they produce nearly all of the world's gold. It will be their duty-and the future peace of the world depends upon whether they perform their duty-to see to it that the new world in which we hope to live is brought into being. One of the most important considerations will be that of currency, and another -that of food. The united nations have said, and particularly Mr. Morgenthau on behalf of the United States treasury, that the international currency of the future will be based on gold. In view of that, I do not see how we can possibly any longer ignore gold prospecting and discovery.
Mining is a wasting asset. The mining industry is decreasing, and at this very hour is in grave danger. Unless the government takes steps immediately to enourage people to enter that industry, andi to encourage mines to use their surpluses in developing the country, we shall have a northland of ghost towns, and the dead-hand of decay will be laid on what must be, if we are to prosper, the greatest and brightest spot in the Canadian economy.
